questions.q: What does it mean that a Spark DataFrame is 'distributed'?
options: It's really a description of data spread across many partitions on many Executors, not sitting in one place
It exists in exactly one place, just like a Pandas DataFrame
It cannot be filtered or grouped like a normal table
It is stored permanently on a single hard drive
questions.explain: This is precisely what lets a Spark DataFrame grow beyond the single-machine memory limit Lesson 28 described.

questions.q: What does 'immutable' mean for a Spark DataFrame?
options: A transformation never modifies the original DataFrame — it always returns a distinct new one
The DataFrame can never be read more than once
Immutable means the DataFrame has no columns
Immutable is just another word for 'lazy'
questions.explain: This is different from how Pandas code often feels, even though Pandas itself also technically creates new objects in many cases.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what happens to the original df after calling df.filter(...)?
options: df remains completely unchanged; the filtered result is a separate, new DataFrame
df is deleted entirely
df is modified in place to match the filtered result
df and the filtered DataFrame become identical, sharing the same object
questions.explain: This is confirmed by df.count() still returning the original row count after filtering.

questions.q: What genuinely carries over from Pandas to Spark DataFrames, according to this lesson?
options: The concepts — rows, columns, schema, filtering, grouping — transfer directly; Chapter 4 mostly teaches new syntax for ideas already understood
Nothing at all carries over — Spark DataFrames are completely unrelated to anything in Chapter 2
Only the exact same method names carry over, with no conceptual similarity
Pandas skills are actively counterproductive when learning Spark
questions.explain: This is meant to be reassuring — Chapter 4 builds on real understanding already developed, not starting from scratch.

questions.q: Why does immutability matter for how you write Spark code?
options: You must capture a transformation's result in a new variable (or reassign the same name) rather than expecting the original DataFrame to change
It means you should never assign the result of a transformation to any variable
It has no practical effect on how code is actually written
It means every Spark script can only ever create exactly one DataFrame
questions.explain: This is a direct consequence of immutability that affects real, everyday PySpark code.
